utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, before we begin today, there is an oral ruling the Chamber wishes to make. With respect to the accused's motion to postpone the evidence of witness KDZ 492, filed on 27th of September 2011, the Chamber has considered both the arguments raised in the motion and the Prosecution's response provided orally on the same day. While mindful of the fact that the witness is already here, the Chamber has decided to grant the motion and postpone his evidence to the week of 17th of October. In reaching its decision, the Chamber took into account the fact that the evidence of KDZ 492 and KDZ 532 may overlap to some extent, meaning that the evidence of KDZ 532 may be of relevance to the accused's preparation for the evidence of KDZ 492. The Chamber also took into account that both KDZ 492 and KDZ 532 are delayed disclosure witnesses, whose relatively voluminous evidence was disclosed to the accused only recently. In that respect, it is of significance that the materials relating to KDZ 532 were disclosed to the accused in a piecemeal fashion and that, while the transcript of his interviews were disclosed on 21st of September, the related Rule 68 material was disclosed only yesterday, as was the Rule 66(B) material. While the Chamber agrees with the accused could have discovered the connection between the two witnesses already on 21st of September, when KDZ 532's identity was disclosed to him, the Chamber is also mindful that not all of the material relating to KDZ 532 - and thus potentially relevant to KDZ 492 - was disclosed to the accused on that day. For that reason, the Chamber has decided to grant the motion. So in this regard, Mr. Tieger, given this ruling and for the purpose of the smooth running of this trial in the future, the Prosecution may wish to consider scheduling the delayed disclosure witnesses in such a way that allows the accused time to prepare for them, in particular in cases where they may be related to each other. That said, sir, if you could stand and take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us your full name, please, then?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: My name is Nusret Sivac, born 19 August 19947 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivac. Now, Mr. Sivac, did you testify here at this Tribunal in the case against Milomir Stakic on July 29, 30, and 31, and the 1st of August 2002, and then again on 13 January 2003?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In preparing to give evidence here today, did you have a chance to listen to a recording of that testimony from 2002 and 2003?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as far as you recall, was it accurate?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: For the most part, everything was correct, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I was to ask you the same questions you were asked at that time, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would give almost the same answers, although I would add to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the addition you've just referred to, was that in regard to the members of a delegation that you described as visiting Omarska at pages 6639 to 6647 of your transcript?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, maybe we will just turn to that very quickly, then. In your transcript, you describe the visit of Serbian officials to Omarska while you were held prisoner there, and you mentioned seeing a number of people or recognising a number of people within that delegation; Simo Drljaca, Milorad Vukic, Radoslav Brdjanin, Mico Kovacevic, Milomir Stakic, Srjdo Srdic, Simo Miskovic, Milan Andzic, Radmilo Zeljaja, and Dusan Kovacevic [sic]. Now, in addition to the names that I've just listed, did you see anyone else in the delegation you recognised?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In that evidence at that trial, I was answering a specific question from the Prosecutor, namely which high-ranking politicians and officials visited the Omarska camp. I said it was Radoslav Brdjanin. And then the next question focused on local Prijedor politicians who were part of that visit, so I left unsaid who from that political delegation from Banja Luka was there and I will say that now: Along with Radoslav Brdjanin, who was the highest ranking official to ever visit Omarska camp, at that time he was at the head of the Autonomous Province of Bosnian Krajina, there was Radislav Vukic also known as Rade the monster.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sivac, I've just given you those names and I'll repeat them again for you, the names that you gave in your previous testimony, and then I'll give you my question again. You said in the Stakic proceedings that you saw Brdjanin, Vukic, Drljaca, Kovacevic, Stakic, Srdic, Miskovic, Milan Andzic, Radmilo Zeljaja and Dusan Kovacevic [sic]. In addition to those people, was there anyone else in the delegation you recognised?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In your first enumeration, there is a mistake. It's not Milorad Vukic but it's Milorad Vokic. He was always accompanying Brdjanin in Prijedor. You should correct Vukic to Vokic. But that political delegation from Banja Luka included along with Brdjanin, Radoslav Vukic, the president of the Serbian Democratic Party in Banja Luka, then Radic who was at the head of the Banja Luka municipality, and Stojan Zupljanin. Those were the political officers who came directly from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And actually, I have only one other question related to your evidence in the Stakic case. I saw that at page 10270, my former colleague referred you to an incident on a day in late July when 12 buses, late July 1992, when 12 buses of men from the Brdo region arrived in the Omarska camp. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Sometime after the 20th of July, we heard that there was ethnic cleansing on the left bank of the Sana river, where a series of Muslim villages were situated, Zecovi, Carakovo, Biscani, near Srdica -- Srdica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the first three or four.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the next day, the very next day, buses started arriving at Omarska. Since I was in a room with Burho and Mujo, the detainees who were being brought from Brdo were being lined up and they were very badly treated. We called that very thin wall the Wailing Wall or the wall of tears. Only in those two days, according to Berko and Mujo who used to go in and out of that room, along with a group of other inmates to clear the blood stains and other traces of mistreatment on that wall, to the horrible yelling of the guards at those people who were brought from Brdo, they were very badly, inhumanely treated. Some people who were brought from Brdo were killed immediately during that admission process, as the guards called it. The guards would come and make inmates use firefighters' hoses to try to get those blood stains off the wall. They said, those inmates, that 12 buses full of people had arrived and there were large numbers of people killed and they were all lying on the ground. And one day he came with a big stick and I asked him, "What is that?" And he said, "This is the stick -- the staff that belonged to my neighbour, Zenkic. He won't need it any more because he's lying there dead next to the house."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, if we can just go back to the very beginning of your answer for a couple of minutes, I have a couple of additional questions for you, all right? First of all, you talked about -- you said sometime after 20 July we heard there was ethnic cleansing on the left bank of the Sana river where a series of Muslim villages were situated, but you were speaking the names of those villages too quickly for my colleagues in the booth to interpret them. Could you just repeat only those village names, please?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We in Prijedor called these villages Brdo as a group. They were in one line. That's Zecovi, Carakovo, Hambarine, Rakovcani, Rizvanovici, Biscani, and Sredica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Witness, you talked about buses arriving at Omarska and referred to detainees being brought from Brdo, lined up, and being badly treated. Can you just clarify who was on the buses?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, the villagers from the villages I just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how do you know they were on the buses?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, we heard that from the guards, and also a few days later, when they appeared in the lines for food distribution, and we recognised some of -- old acquaintances from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, moving at too great a pace, Your Honour. I'll like to tender the 92 ter transcript of this witness, which is 65 ter number 22701, please, as a Prosecution exhibit, and I should note that there is a small bit of that testimony that was recorded in private session, and we've prepared a redacted version. We have accordingly prepared a redacted version, 65 ter number 22701B is the public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both versions will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour 65 ter 22701 shall be given Exhibit P3477 under seal. And 22701B shall be given Exhibit P3478 and is admitted publicly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we come to the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, would Your Honour like me to read the associated exhibit numbers out or shall I deal with that with my colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd prefer to follow the latter suggestion, but I have a question in relation to four documents which are -- have been allegedly tendered for reference only. If you could clarify the meaning?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As I was reading the transcript, Your Honour, I saw that the president at that time had asked for colour versions of the exhibit numbers previously admitted, and those were accordingly given separate -- those versions, which are in any other -- in all other ways identical, were given separate exhibit numbers. I'm in Your Honour's hands as to how you would prefer to deal with that. I just thought to have the transcript clear, there could be a document linked to the number that the president at that time was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is evident from the transcript itself that they are duplicates of another one. So I don't think we need to admit it at all. And shall I come back to the -- one of the original? 5772.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure how it forms an indispensable and inseparable part of the transcript. According to the transcript, the witness just read out and nothing was asked about this article. And same seems to be true at the 65 ter number 11740. So if you are minded to tender those articles, I would recommend you to explore those articles with the witness yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would I be able to do that now, then, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 05772, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the documents are being uploaded, I forgot to ask you, Mr. Robinson, whether there is any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, and you're taking care of this issue quite well, better than we could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you able to read Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm a little bit hesitant. I hear a delay when I'm speaking in the microphone today. Do you see the article on the left-hand side of the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Representatives of Krajina in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this article? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. In the trial of Stakic. It was shown to make clearer the situation around that visit to the camp by the delegation, the Presiding Judge let me read this article from Kozarski Vjesnik and another one from Glas of Banja Luka. I read those texts and they showed who was on that delegation from Banja Luka and from Prijedor so that my first statement, when I mentioned only Radoslav Brdjanin, was complemented by the reading of these articles. And it was not necessary then for me to repeat those names.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you some brief questions about this article? You said that this article is from Kozarski Vjesnik. Could you explain what kind of media Kozarski Vjesnik is?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, Kozarski Vjesnik was the main propaganda vehicle that Serbian politicians in Prijedor used to put out proclamations and pamphlets. On the 30th of April, and after the takeover, after the military coup --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you. You've answered my question. I would just like to move on to another question about this article. Is the name of this journal in the bold print at the top left-hand of this page in front of you? Do you see the words Kozarski Vjesnik headlined on the top left of the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just stamped on top of the letters OZ is something that we can't quite read. Are you able to distinguish what that says?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I think it says that this is a wartime edition. At the time they referred to the editions of Kozarski Vjesnik as wartime editions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this article refers to a visit or visits by Radoslav Brdjanin, Radoslav Vukic, Stojan Zupljanin, and Predrag Radic to Prijedor on 17 July 1992. Now, to your recollection, are these persons some of the same persons who formed part of the delegation that visited Omarska camp that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Along the political -- alongside the political delegation there was a group of journalists from Banja Luka who did their utmost to convey their story in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If that could be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 79, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see 11740 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, you see here another issue of Kozarski Vjesnik dated 26 June 1992, and the story on the bottom left-hand corner of the page is the story I'd like to draw your attention to. It's entitled, "Monster Doctor." Have you seen this article before?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with anyone from the Prijedor area who had the nickname Monster Doctor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor were completely controlled by the SDS in Prijedor. Through their broadcasts and issues, they turned on prominent Banja Luka citizens accusing them of different types of crimes. However, all those people were decent citizens of Prijedor. All those whose names were called out, so to say, by means of Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor were basically marked to be killed, as they eventually were in the various camps. This particular article concerns Osman Mahmuljin, a Prijedor physician, who specialised in internal medicine. There is an interesting thing about Prijedor. At the helm of the municipality of Prijedor, there were two physicians, Milomir Stakic and Mico Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sivac, I'd just like to ask you one question about Mr. Mahmuljin who is referred to in this article. What happened to Mr. Mahmuljin? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We were taken to Omarska together. In late July he was killed there, during a systematic process of execution of prominent Prijedor citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as Exhibit P3480. So with the exception of those four exhibits, that was tendered for reference. All the other exhibits will be admitted and given numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Ms. Edgerton, given that this witness's evidence was tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter, why don't you offer the summary of this witness's evidence for the benefit of the public, if you are ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed I'm ready Your Honour, I apologise, I'm quite disconcerted by the delay in my microphone today, and I would like to do that. Mr. Nusret Sivac is a Bosnian Muslim who until 1989 worked for the Public Security Services in Prijedor and in 1992 was working as a television reporter in the same area. His written evidence provides an overview of the armed Serb takeover of Prijedor in April 1992, and the Serb attack on the area and consequent ethnic cleansing which began on 30 May 1992. He has given evidence about the persecution of non-Serbs and the destruction of non-Serb religious buildings and property. He was arrested by Serb police on 10 June 1992, and taken to Keraterm and Omarska but released the same day. He was again arrested on 20 June 1992 and returned to Omarska. He describes the brutal, inhumane conditions for huge numbers of non-Serbs in prison there, including himself, women as well as men. The prisoners were beaten, tortured and killed, barely fed. Women were brutally abused. In July 1992, Mr. Sivac saw a delegation of Bosnian Serb officials who he recognised visit the camp. That day, he was lined up with the rest of the camp population and made to sing Serbian songs and in front of the visitors. He was transferred to -- he was transferred to Trnopolje camp in August 1992 where he remained for 14 days. On his release he returned to Prijedor where he remained until being finally able to leave in December 1992 after signing over all his property. And just before -- having concluded the summary, just before I finally take my seat, I note that when I asked Mr. Sivac the question about the members of the delegation, the second time, I omitted one of the names of the delegation members. Dusan Jankovic was omitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivac, your testimony given at the Stakic trial was admitted in its entirety, and then you will be further asked by the accused, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that your evidence is quite voluminous, I'll strive to put short and simple questions which for the most part could be answered with a "yes" or "no." By the same token, please pause between questions and answers, as I will too, so that the interpreters could catch up. Did you serve your military term?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you complete a course during your term?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I did. As a radio mechanic for military radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of education did this course give you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: As part of that course for radio mechanics, when there were military call-ups, I always served as a military radio mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean a signalsman?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my military specialty too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this also entail working on teleprinters and other equipment, including coding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we try again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think either of us was rude or untoward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I did attend courses in coding and telefax operation but only once I was received -- or employed by the state security in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you work for the public or the state security?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I worked in the communications and encoding centre, which was part of the Public Security Service under the new structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did not work in state security?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, never. In some of my earlier statements I found it to be a mistake, something that was wrongly recorded. There seems to be a mix-up between the public and State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am confused by that as well because in one of the statements we can find that you worked for the State Security Service, you also had your code name and took care of Tito's safety when he went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I have to expand on that. We in the communications centre, we did have nicknames or code names, if you will. We all worked as team when Tito was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we were at our work posts. I forgot what your first question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the statement from 1994, we see that you worked in the secret service and that you alone and your boss had access to certain material and that you were answerable to the federal secretariat and to the military courts rather than civilian courts and that you also took care of Tito's safety and the safety of other prominent persons on visit in Bosnia. It is page 3 of the 1994 statement. It also says that as a secret agent, your code name was K-5 Joja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this expanded question of yours is an argument. You took it out of the context of something I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you started working as a camera man, did you also work for the police simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, for a while I worked in parallel for the state security -- Public Security Service and radio-television Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your proper job and what was your auxiliary job?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I was employed in full at an accelerated rate of accrual of the number of years in the public service, Public Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you retire or were you fired?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's wrong information again. Because of certain arguments, I applied for an early retirement. By the time, I was already working for the television. I made use of the right I had to receive an early retirement while continuing to work for radio-television Sarajevo as a correspondent for western Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were not fired but you retired because you had another job as a source of income on top of your pension; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the interethnic conflicts and tensions which came into being in the service, I was basically forced to apply for early retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say basically. Were you or were you not? It is difficult to qualify this basic concept or the concept of basically in legal terms. What did you do exactly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Under the law in the then-Yugoslavia, I could apply for early retirement, and I did so. I started receiving my pension while at the same time continuing as a war correspondent for the Sarajevo TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you applied for retirement, did you also apply due to medical reasons? Did you submit any medical papers which assisted your claim or your application?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It included standard problems experienced by most security service employees. Such problems occur due to shift work and overload. I suffered from insomnia, burnout, and other such symptoms which take place after one had worked in night shift for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The documents were issued by a psychiatrist. What was his conclusion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I have no idea. Together with a group of men from Prijedor, I went to Sarajevo and we had interviews there. Or conversations. After a while, documents arrived granting my request for early retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose you wouldn't object to us producing those documents here without public broadcast?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I do not object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you start again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My microphone was on. I don't know if you can hear me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you said at page 6561 of the transcript, when you said that Milos Jankovic arrived in the service to ethnically cleanse it, but that wouldn't be quite accurate, would it? It is page 11 in e-court and 6561 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. When Milos Jankovic arrived, he assisted greatly in the ethnic cleansing of the service for which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the local police chief, or a local police chief, at any level, had the authority to change the ethnic composition of the force or would this have been something to be approved at a level of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: When Milos Jankovic arrived in the service, he was actually one of the main reasons for my early retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you gain that information? Was this some sort of information or was it an impression of yours that Milos Jankovic was tasked with ethnically cleansing the service? Do you base your claim on a document or is this merely an impression?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It is part of my knowledge which I base on facts. In the service, we kept a close watch of the ethnic makeup of the force. There were nine employees, and we always paid attention to the number of Muslims and Serbs on the force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are the facts which made you conclude that you were retired because of your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The best employee in the service was Veso [as interpreted] Vojnikovic. He was a workmate who was forced to retire following a banal incident. Another person was employed instead of him, who was a Serb. Milos Jankovic brought Ranko Kovacevic to the service without any authority. According to all the regulations and laws in place for the service, such a person ought not to have been employed there. He had a criminal -- disciplinary file. He was a simple policeman, of very modest education. Instead of being driven out of the security service for engaging in a number of dodgy deals, he was brought to our service to work side by side with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that Milos Jankovic had the authority to employ or fire people in the service, which is highly centralised and follows strict procedures of admission which are not available to any job candidates?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It was pursuant to his proposal that our service was manned. He was the one who put forth proposals to the chief of the service as to who should be employed in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were checks and that there was a certain period of time which had to elapse before someone is employed and that such procedures go up to the level of the ministry, along the various department lines, in order to grant the vetting procedure?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Not quite. Ranko Kovacevic instead of being fired was employed in our service to work for -- I'm not sure who. I guess he was there to control what the rest of us did and noted down. To use the simple terminology, he was supposed to monitor us. I have said already that an operator working on codes in any particular shift was the only person entitled to receive certain dispatches in order to forward them to the appropriate services to which they were addressed. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make your conclusions based on one person being fired and one person being employed, when you say that Mr. Jankovic came there to cleanse the service? Or do you have any other proof?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Following Esad Vojnikovic, I was the next to leave the service. And again, my post was taken up by a Serb. At the end, on the eve of the war, there was only one Muslim in the office left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the issue of whether you were fired or retired, and you said you were not fired. You said you retired.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. But Mr. Karadzic, Milos Jankovic and the chief of the security service were supposed to find a replacement for me, to bring a Muslim to the communications and encoding centre, a person of appropriate background and education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that before 1990, before the multi-party elections, Milos Jankovic could implement nationalist policies in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which the most senior positions were occupied by Muslims and Croats since 1967? Are you basically saying that during the communist era, Jankovic could replace people along ethnic lines rather than some other lines?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it proved to be true. Milos Jankovic followed the ethnic line or the ethnic policy. Again, you're taking things out of the context. I don't know to what extent you are familiar with our work. The security service in Prijedor, until a certain time, was fully Serb. Following Sadikovic, I was the third or fourth Bosniak, Muslim, to be employed in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you discussing now the post-war period, and does it have anything to do with the participation of Muslims in the Ustasha army and that this was the cause of distrust?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I am well acquainted with the history of Prijedor. In Prijedor, in the area of Prijedor, there were no people who joined Ustasha forces. Or if there were, that number was negligible. Everyone was on the side of the liberation movement and supported partisans and wanted to chase the fascists away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Dzafer Kulenovic. Does he not hail from that area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. And I was referring to Prijedor alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you work for the counter-intelligence service in order to break-up Croatian nationalism in 1973 as it says in your statement? But I believe that Croatian spring concluded in 1971, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In that statement I mentioned when I joined the service, and I said that there were still people around who had participated in the infamous Croatian Spring. My service, as other security services in the area of Prijedor, wanted to see those people brought before courts. You know that any police work is team work. It means that both Public and State Security Service, as well as all other segments, work as a team in order to deal with state enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it is not correct that you worked for the counter-intelligence service or is it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. This is just a paraphrase, and I don't know who authored that paraphrase. I never stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your 1994 statement, on page 3 and page 4. At that time, in the same capacity, did you also persecute members of Cominform Bureau who appeared in 1948? Was it not late for you to pursue Cominform members in 1968?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, a group of Cominform members appeared in Prijedor. They organised their meetings there. One of them was Gojko Biljajac, my closest neighbour in the building where I resided. He had already been sentenced to imprisonment on Goli island as a member of Cominform. Together with him in that group, there was also Dr. Orlic from Bosanska Dubica. This may be of some interest for this Trial Chamber. She was the wife of the chief of security in Bosanska Dubica, and they were indeed involved in organising and reactivating the group of Cominform in Prijedor and in Bosanska Dubica and that is why they were punished to long prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you, as a communication officer, how did you figure in all that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In the centre, I did my every day duties, and I had a group of operatives who had arrived from Sarajevo. They gave me a task to monitor the situation in my building, or rather to follow the activities of Gojko Biljajac who was a suspect. I was supposed to monitor his movements and to inform people from Sarajevo about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those were people from Sarajevo, from the state security, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did they not tell you that a person from public security should not work for state security under the law?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I was not officially employed by the state security. I just did them a favour. At that moment they saw me as the most reliable person and least conspicuous person. If they had attempted to install their own man, Gojko Biljajac, who was a dissident, would have found that suspicious. The building was very small and it had a small number of apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that means that you worked -- unofficially you were a spy as it were, you monitored the behaviour of people on behalf of the state security while you were still an employee of the public security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that that's against the law?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, that was the only case, the case of Gojko Biljajac and the group of Cominform members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a communist?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but I would like to add something in my answer to the previous question, just briefly. It is not correct that we who worked in the communication centres were not allowed to work for the state security. In the Prijedor SUP there was a detachment of the state security. The main office was in Banja Luka. And in our line of work, we worked quite extensively for the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are saying that it is not against the law for the two services to mix up?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You're referring to that plenum when Ranko was removed. Let me tell you, Mr. Karadzic, in my job, and I worked for a long time in public security, we worked quite extensively for the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were a communist, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a very convinced loyal, hardened communist? What kind of a communist were you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. I accepted the ideology because that's the way my parents were, and you know, to take up such a responsible position you had to be a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I find some other things confusing at the moment. Is it correct that you were retired after you had put forth a defiant proposal to the personnel service, that person was a Muslim, and it was absolutely out of the question for that person to be employed, and that move was taken against you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I was involved in an informal conversation with a group of colleagues, police officers, and they asked me what I thought who should be the chief of the Public Security Service. My answer was, well, this time it should be a Muslim, and they held it against me. They thought that it was a mistake on my part, based on my ethnic feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you also mention the name of that person that would be appropriate for that position?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So in 1980 and 1981, you behaved quite responsibly and you monitored the ethnic composition of employees in Prijedor. You counted heads. Wasn't that a bit premature for a member of the Communist Party, to count heads along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count people because of that. That was just something that I perceived. That was my impression and the impression was that in the security service the other ethnic groups are not well enough represented. I never said it in public. I never voiced my opinion publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it seems that at the time you were embittered, that you were full of bitterness, you were not satisfied?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, no. I was never embittered with the system which I served loyally until the 1st of January 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to hear from you whether there was either an official or an unofficial commission that could say who was a good Muslim and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know whether the qualifications of Muslims that we found in your statements and in your books, did you take them over from an official organisation or a commission, or are these your own qualifications of those people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The only thing I had were my own impressions, and I was the only one who could be the judge of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you said about a Muslim whose wife was Serb, that he was a reserve Muslim.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In late 1991, on the eve of the first democratic elections, a man became the head of security. His name was Sead Besic, and I qualified him as a reserve Muslim. That's how I described him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your book, you mention quite a large number of Muslims whom you considered traitors because they remained living and working with the Serbs in Prijedor, whereas you thought that that was not okay, that that should not be done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. It's not correct. I published a list of Muslims who killed other Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 243 of your book, you wrote that: "Muslims Were Committing Crimes Against Their Own People." That's the title. And the subtitle is: "Traitors Who Killed Their Own People," and you provide a list of at least 15 people in Prijedor, including Sead Besic, who was a police officer, or rather a member of the state security. Then also Hamdija Handzic, also a Muslim, a major in the Serb artillery who stayed in the Serb Army; Zijad Music; Asmir Music; Zlatan Blazevic, also known as Laja; Atko Blazevic, also known as Leri - the last two were Croats - Emso Sabic, Sabo; Sabahudin Zulic, also known as Butko; Goran Egrlic - all Muslims but the two Croats - another person, a lady called Karalic, a Muslim; and then Ernest Badnjevic; Zlatan Crnalic [phoen]; Muhamed Sarajlic; Said Alabegovic [phoen]; and Zlatan Selimbegovic. You listed them as people who were traitors because they remained living with the Serbs as members of the Serb army or the Serb bodies of authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. It is not. Mr. Karadzic, I did not put them on the list of traitors because they served loyally in the Serb army, but because of the fact that as members of the Serb army, they went and killed people in Bihac, Gradacac, along the corridor, and in all the other parts where the elite Prijedor troops went to wage war. That means that Muslims killed other Muslims. So how should they be qualified but as traitors? There was just one word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. You deny them the right to foster political differences. Were Serbs not killing other Serbs in the Second World War? Did partisans and Chetniks kill each other or did they not?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm talking about the period that I survived. Let us leave history to talk about the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you have just told us that these Muslims killed other Muslim people. Did they go there to fight against the Muslim army or against the Muslim people? Do you have any proof that any of these people who were obviously in favour of Yugoslavia and in favour of living together with the Serbs, that they killed people and not the troops?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, if we're talking about the traitors of Muslim people who I've listed here, I can write their autobiographies. Your Honours, my explanations would take too long, and I don't want to waste your time. In all of my previous statements, I stated what I did and I adhere by my words. Among these people that Mr. Karadzic has just named, there are also some people from the margins of life, criminals, who did not care about any ideology. From the Serb army, they received weapons and they could legally go and kill other people, loot their homes, beat them, and that was their pay for what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We did not see that, Mr. Sivac, anywhere, no media has ever mentioned that, let alone court documents. But tell me, if you say that they are traitors, what would they say about you? That you're a Muslim extremist, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I would like you to ask them. I would like to hear their opinion. Why don't you ask them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Zlatan Crnalic, who is a graduate of the air force academy is a criminal in your view?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I said some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, who did the Muslim journalists kill? One of them is Said Hadziahmetovic, he was a male, a journalist, an editor-in-chief in the Serb radio; Dinka Tatarevic, a journalist; Jadranka Vejo [phoen], she is a Muslim; Samija Dzafic [phoen], a Muslim; and Muharem Hasakurtovic [phoen], also a Muslim. They're all journalists and you also put them on the blacklist, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Those people worked in Radio Prijedor and Kozarski Vjesnik, and I provided a general statement, and I said that Radio Prijedor and Kozarski Vjesnik were the worst kind of propaganda machinery acting on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party, and their false propaganda was something that even Goebbels could envy them. And in general terms, through the newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik and on the radio, many respectable citizens of Prijedor were named and later on killed in camps around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, is it correct, however, that you concluded that all Serbs, irrespective of their party affiliation, had opted for the politics of the reorganisation of Bosnia, the reorganisation of Prijedor, and you yourself stated in the book and in the statements, that there was no difference between the leftist Serbs, the rightist Serbs, the communists, the reformists, that they were all members of the Crisis Staff, that they all pursued the same politics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as Prijedor is concerned, it was really not important whether people indeed held the idea of the Serbian Democratic Party. All the Serbs were on the same side and their only goal was for the Prijedor municipality to be ethnically cleansed from all those who were not Serbs, and they were all very fervently working towards that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that Radio Prijedor was a tool of propaganda of the SDS, it would be better to say that Radio Prijedor was the propaganda tool of the Serbian people, is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, both would be correct. But Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor were under the direct control of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you see that Muslims were also employed there. You even say that Jadranka published with some joy that the Serb Democratic Party had taken control over Prijedor on the 30th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. She was born in a mixed marriage, and she lived in a mixed marriage, and that was her private opinion. And yes, she still works in Prijedor, she is still a journalist affiliated with Radio Prijedor, and she is a good journalist, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, she is also one of those reserve Muslims, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, you said that. I would tell her that if we were to find each other face-to-face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we will take a break now, for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] It could have been said in public, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very much so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we are bringing in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I became slightly clearer about your attitude to Muslims. I would like to clear up your attitude to the Serbs. There are things that still confuse me about that. Did you really write that Serbs are criminals and bloodthirsty?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, considering all that I've been through and all the events I witnessed, it's possible that in some of my writings I did indeed write that, but, Mr. Karadzic, I go to Prijedor nowadays and I spend a lot of time there and I continue to see my Serb friends. I have coffee with them and a long, nice talk. I don't communicate only with those Serbs who have blood on their hands. In fact, I divide people into human and non-human. I don't divide them into Muslim, Serbs, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, on the pages 19 and 20 of your book, before the war in Bosnia, you say on page 19, that Serbs took pleasure in the air strikes against hospitals and kindergartens, and on page 20 you wrote: "How can these children wage war against these bloodthirsty Serbs armed to their teeth?" You wrote that before the war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I'd like to see it. If you have a transcript in B/C/S, I'd like to see exactly what I wrote and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your book, pages 19 and 20. Did you write a book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: But what's the context, what kind of events am I talking about? Oh, you mean the war in Croatia that I followed with my TV crew?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Those were my impressions from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in your reporting from Croatia, you, as a reporter, sided fully with the Croatian secession, and you reported in a very biased way against the Serbs, according to Serbian evaluation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's not the case at all. You misinterpreted and misrepresented completely, trying to accuse me of something that I'm not guilty of. It was an agreement between the editorial board of my newspaper and the Television Sarajevo. I was always accompanied by Boro Grubic, a Serb reporter, whenever I went into the battlefield. That was an agreement made because Boro Grubic was a fantastic commentator. In the war in Croatia, I only worked as a cameraman. All the political comment was done by a Serb, Boro Grubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, and in your book, you never mention, let alone highlight, the large numbers of refugees from Croatia. In 1991, in Prijedor and Banja Luka, weren't there so many refugees from Croatia, including lots of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. There were not that many in Prijedor. And I remember in 1991, together with my colleague Boro Grubic, I was filming a report about those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm confused because you never mention it in your book or in the testimony recorded in the transcripts. But there is another thing that confuses me. On page 71 of your book, you say: "This is typical only of Serbs. They are always extreme, both when it's time to be a nationalist and when it's time to be communist, when it's time to be Godless, or a religious fundamentalist. They are very quick to embrace completely opposite ideologies. The only thing that matters is that they are constantly opposed to other people and that their turn-coat policy brings them advantage."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I was just stating facts. Until very recently, people who used to be extreme communists, hard-line communists, changed -- turned coat completely with the appearance of nationalist parties, and I knew that that would never bring anything good to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was not a slip of the tongue, it was not said by chance? I was hoping it was. Look at what you wrote about the 2nd of September 1991. I was really astonished by this. You say that soldiers and office at some sort of celebration, a welcome ceremony, organised for them by the Serbs in the settlement of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic be asked to read slowly? We don't have this text and we cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to catch you up a while ago. Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 21 of your book, writing about 2 September 1991, you describe attending a welcome ceremony that the people organised for a tank battalion, a so-called popular luncheon, and you write that soldiers and officers are hungrily eating roast pork, drinking local brandy, and hopping and dancing and skipping. Isn't this rather offensive to speak like that, saying that they are drinking hooch by the gallons, and isn't the wheel dance they were dancing, the Kozara wheel dance, also your traditional dance?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I was just describing what I was seeing. And in writing those lines, I was so disenchanted by the conduct of the Yugoslav Army that had come to the area of Prijedor from Croatia and turned all their artillery and other guns against Muslim-populated areas, and that army, in which I served loyally once upon a time, became a mono-ethnic one, and that this national -- or nationalist gathering, they made no bones about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on that 2nd of September, you were not able to see that the JNA had trained their guns against any Muslim settlements, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, already, after the withdrawal of the already-defeated, broken Yugoslav Army from Croatia, or just a little later, a large number of artillery and other units stationed themselves in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that on the 30th of May Croatia was still part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was, but I followed the entire war in Croatia, and that formerly Yugoslav Army had become completely mono-ethnic. In Croatia, it defended and protected only the Serb insurgents, and it actively participated in the creation of the so-called Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in July and August 1991, there was a historic Muslim-Serb agreement on the table, initially proposed by Muhamed Filipovic and Adil Zulfikarpasic with the support of Alija Izetbegovic and it was accepted by the Serbian side, it was on the table for all of two months until the end of August?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. Those plans about the restructuring of Bosnia-Herzegovina were numberless, and so were peace conferences, but it was impossible to reconcile two sides that were so completely opposed. The Serbs from Bosnia were ultimative in their demands that Serbs and Serb areas in Bosnia remain part of rump Yugoslavia, whereas all the others, Muslims and Croats, were in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina becoming an independent and sovereign state, which was ultimately accepted by the Badinter commission, and Bosnia was indeed internationally recognised, and on the 22nd of May 1992, it was admitted as a fully fledged UN member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That much is true, but tell us, Mr. Sivac, did the Serbs ever revise their position and did they make concessions? Didn't we accept that Bosnia become an independent state on one condition, accepted by the international community, and that was cantonisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Those were just interim proposals made by you to gain time so that you can create the right setting for what would happen in April 1992, for grabbing and carving out a large chunk of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to annex it to the Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you base this opinion on? You should be talking about facts, not your opinions. Is it a fact, and in that case, what do you base it on?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I base it all on the events that would follow, and I will be speaking only about my municipality of Prijedor, where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. We are still in 1991. Is it true that in your book on page 18 you wrote that Muhamed Cehajic, president of the municipality, and Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, president of the SDA, came out in mid-August and put up barriers in the way of the JNA so they can't move through Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That was reported by both Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor. In fact, there was this tank unit that came to Prijedor and was setting itself up there, without informing the legal representatives of Prijedor municipality; whereas by all the rules, the military command should have informed the representatives of the municipality and the authorities that they would be doing that. Indignant over such a manner of conduct by that military unit, Muhamed Cehajic, who was the legal representative of the municipal authorities, and Mirza Mujadzic tried to put up some roadblocks. However, from the neighbouring houses, Serbs came out already very well armed and Cehajic and Mujadzic withdrew. But the very next day, the military command from Prijedor sent out a communique saying, in no uncertain terms, that they were stationed in Prijedor at the invitation of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivac. But could you please produce that communique testifying to the great love between the JNA and the SDS? But is there a single country in the world where half of the municipal authorities would come out and stand in the way of the only legal armed force in that country?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That happened at that time because strange things were happening in Prijedor. Then generally, in 1991, towards the end of that year, we received reports that at Urije, which is a Serbian neighbourhood in Prijedor, legally elected representatives of the authorities of Serb ethnicity were meeting separately, making some sort of plans for taking over power in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. Let me first ask you this: Do you know that the JNA was a legal and legitimate armed force until the 19th of May 1992, and that Izetbegovic, Kljujic and I, on 23 December 1991, held meetings and begged them to stay and help prevent interethnic conflict? And that was reported by the media.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I remember that. But this spontaneous incident created by Professor Cehajic and Mirza Mujadzic was something that they believed they should do, and they did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, for a president of a party, and a president of the municipality, to act spontaneously and spontaneously confront the army, I find that rather confusing. But let's leave that aside. Is it true that the police blocked military representatives from removing, taking over, the military documentation they needed to carry out mobilisation and call up recruits?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: For the first time, a Muslim came to that position, the head of the military department, Becir Medunjanin came to that position. It was always previously occupied by the Serbs. And before that, Serbs were not mobilised. They volunteered at the military department to go to war in Croatia. Once, outside the SUP and outside the security service, the same premises shared by the military department, the military police came one day and they wanted to remove the files of military conscripts by force. And that's when this minor incident occurred. I don't know how it all developed later, but I know that a large number of Serbs did respond to the mobilisation to go to war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in addition to individual draft calls, there is also such a thing as a general call-up, whereby people are asked by, or through the media to report to certain locations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the entire infrastructure and documentation in this regard belonged to the federal Secretariat for National Defence and that the employee in the municipality was actually employed by the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know the legal definitions, but I do know that once the national parties came to power, Becir Medunjanin, who was an SDA member, was assigned to the post of chief of the military department in Prijedor. I don't know, though, who he reported to. I do think, though, that he had to have been in touch with the republican TO staff or with a command or the command of a military district in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, with the TO staff and the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by a Serb general, Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know who the person in charge was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Becir Medunjanin well?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I met him for the first time when the SDA carried the elections, when he was appointed to his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are the names of his sons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: One is Hanis [phoen], and the one who was killed, well, I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does he have a son who lives in the US?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know where that son is. I used to know him when he was very young.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hanis and Adis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You are saying that. I only know of Hanis, the older one, and I remember having met him somewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Adis Medunjanin was arrested in the US as an Islamic terrorist?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Becir Medunjanin instigated Muslims from Prijedor to fight? He actively assisted in their organisation as part of their preparations for war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: So you say. Do you think, though, that there is a lot there which isn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 21 of your book you say that the ruling SDA in Prijedor would not allow the conscription commission to access the files. Was the SDA the only party in power in Prijedor or was there a coalition in place, including the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. In Prijedor municipality, the SDA won the most votes in the elections, and the next party in line was the SDS. And I believe they split the power in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that Prijedor was predominantly populated by Muslims, and according to the census, there were 49.454 Muslims in 1991; whereas, there were 47.745 Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That data comes from some earlier documents. But the difference in terms of percentage between Serbs and Muslims was some 2 per cent in favour of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the 6.000 plus Yugoslavs? Did you include them in any of the categories?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I did not, they simply proclaimed themselves Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that in 1991, Yugoslavia and declaring oneself as Yugoslav was not a favourable option and that at least four fifths of the Yugoslavs were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Says you, Mr. Karadzic. Among the Yugoslavs in Prijedor municipality, there were many Muslims who declared themselves Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that our electoral system was founded on the majority system -- sorry, proportionate system for the council of citizens and the majority system for the council of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But do you recall that there was such a thing as the council of municipalities in the Bosnian assembly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in Prijedor, as part of the majority system, a Serb, Svetozar Imanac [phoen] won which clearly indicated that there were more Serbs in Prijedor than Muslims and Croats put together?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And I don't even remember the person you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He was a deputy in the assembly. Is it correct that in Prijedor town, there are several thousand Serbs more than Muslims, including Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: These are your assessments, but I do believe that statistics show otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I'm saying. There were 34.000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly slow down when citing figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please slow down when citing figures and could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the town itself, 34.627 Croats, 1.756 Muslims, and 13.372 Serbs, thirteen thousand nineteen sixty-nine [as interpreted] Yugoslavs. And others such as Ruthenians, Czechs, Italians, amounted to less than 2.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this information, of this data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree, then, that Prijedor was a municipality of all? No one was in any significant majority, although there were the most Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In 1991, it was a common municipality of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Regarding the Kozarac crisis, Radio Prijedor broadcast that the Muslims should withdrew to Prijedor due to wartime activities; whereas, you say that a large number of civilians arrived in Prijedor and that all Prijedor citizens assisted those who had fled the fighting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It is not. On the 24th of May 1992, Radmilo Zeljaja, who was on rampage at the time and in command of the infamous Serb unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait. We'll get to that. We don't want the whole history. Did the radio broadcast such information and did the Serbs invite the Muslims from Kozarac as well as the Serbs to come to the town itself? Did you touch upon that in your book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know how those people from Kozarac arrived but they only arrived after Kozarac had been shelled. They were in front of the sport hall in Prijedor for a while, and then they were put aboard trucks and buses and taken to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, you're saying that in Prijedor, where most of the inhabitants were Serbs and Yugoslavs, the civilians from Kozarac simply arrived there because there had been fighting there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They arrived in Prijedor seeking refuge with their friends and relatives. However, only a few Kozarac inhabitants who had been driven out found refuge with their friends and relatives. Most of them were transported to the camp at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's clear this up. Who received those people in Prijedor, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The Kozarac inhabitants who had been driven away found accommodation in the Puharska settlement in Prijedor, which was predominantly populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those who were driven out of Kozarac, well, this is something that this Defence will have to keep working on, but I'm asking you this specifically: The civilians from Kozarac who either fled or were driven out, we'll see that, did they find accommodation in the town itself, and with whom?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Only a small number of them were accommodated in Puharska with their Muslim friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the Muslims that took them in seemed to have been safe in Prijedor, and these people found refuge with them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but only at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll have to skip topics, but at page 26 of your book, you seem to say that the Serbs destroyed the bridge in Bosanska Dubica, and then in one of the subsequent paragraphs, you say that it was destroyed from the Croatian side. How could the Serbs have crossed over to the Croatian side in order to destroy the bridge? And you seem to say the same thing about all the bridges across the Sava, in other words that they were destroyed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I personally shot from the bridge with my camera, together with my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how do you know who destroyed it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Please do be patient with me. I reported from the -- from the Una valley. I observed how the Serbs from the Krajina were ethnically cleansing the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the bridges now. How can you assert in your book that the Serbs, who lived on one bank of the Sava, destroyed the bridge which connected them with the Serbs living on the other side of the Sava?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Because Jasenovac had been occupied by Martic's soldiers from the Serb Krajina in Croatia. The moment they got into Jasenovac, they torched a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it across the river from Dubica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was occupied by the Knin Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we have the Serbs on both banks of the Sava and yet we have Serbs destroying the bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That was the information we received at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The people who were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it not correct that your acquaintance, Milenko Tubica [phoen], an official of the Bosanska Dubica municipality, complained that the bridge was the cause of isolation of that municipality, so a Serb from the left bank complained of ties being severed with the Serbs on the other side, and yet you still seem to believe that the Serbs destroyed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: My colleague, Boro Grubic, reported on that. And I simply conveyed information he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 32 you say that communists Mico Sarjevic [phoen] and Jaksic from the chamber of commerce arrived. Can we agree that neither of them were SDS members?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what party they belonged to, but I do know that they came to the Prijedor theatre to have an open discussion at which they openly invited the people of Prijedor to join the newly formed autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina. Prijedor has traditional ties to Banja Luka, in terms of friendship, economy, transport and other infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they supported their call by economic reasons, resources, and the need to become independent of Sarajevo, Nedim Kadiric [phoen], a Muslim journalist dispersed the gathering in a way?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He put a few direct questions, which they were unable to answer, and they simply backtracked. They realised they wouldn't do anything in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Prijedor some 30 or 32 kilometres from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. The distance is 55 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By road perhaps, but I meant as the crow flies. With a lot of ill intent, you seem to discuss the issue of reconstructing churches, but you were reluctant to record any footage about that.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. It only concerns the Serb village of Nisevic, near Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next you say that Serbs had a morbid relationship to anything non-Serb. It was at page 37. Such proof of ordered crime is without any shame broadcast by TV stations in Yugoslavia and Belgrade, and in Banja Luka. Can you explain what kind of morbid attitude did Serbs have towards all things unSerb?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Zivko Ecim was the most morbid of all in terms of his reporting from the theatre in Croatia. They recorded Serb soldiers who shelled certain buildings in the area according to their -- to humour them. They made many tapes, and even sold them in Prijedor. Isn't it morbid to ask for a Croatian house to be destroyed so that they could shoot some footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Sivac, you didn't say two men. You said the Serbs. Why didn't you accuse them? They could then defend themselves. They would be able to respond, but you accuse the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Because the Serbs in Prijedor bought the tape en masse and enjoyed watching it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you called me a werewolf from Mount Dermiter [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. Everything is possible. I paraphrased that. I took it from a Sarajevo newspaper, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that a wolf is a correct translation. It should werewolf, a psychiatrist, a werewolf from Dermiter, Radovan Karadzic, whatever his name is, he clearly is -- sends threats from a hole in Sarajevo and said that Muslims should disappear. You are referring to my speech in 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, your attitude towards me, doesn't it disqualify you as a witness? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
