utterances.text: I don't think so. That was the belief at the time when everything started, and I believe that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, among the other ethnic groups, that was the belief. That's -- many from the other ethnic groups saw you that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that we signed a cease-fire with Croats very early on, that Muslims told us everything that we needed to know, well, in time, that we cooperated with Muslims, we had very good relations with them, we had entire Muslim units in our army, and you talk about that in your book, you say that a lot of Muslims were traitors of the SDA politics.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 6th of May 1992, we signed a cease-fire agreement with Muslims and that saved tens of thousands of lives. There was some fighting after that, but to a lesser extent, and do you know that we signed another agreement with Avdic? We didn't fight with him. We even supported him and helped him survive. Do you know that many Muslims from Sarajevo sent us information on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what the Sarajevo kitchen cooked for you, but I know that all the cease-fire agreements and peace agreements that were signed ad hoc were very short-lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that when General Vukosavljevic was removed from a position as the head of the Territorial Defence on the 8th of April, that on the 12th of April, the new commander, Hasan Efendic, issued an order to attack the Bosnian Serbs and the JNA? That was on the 12th of April, and on the 13th of April that order was on my desk, and then we got the admission from the Bosnian Army. I received that on the 13th of April from Muslims who were against the war. Did you hear of that order or that directive?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that order or that directive. This is the first time I hear of it. I heard of a dispatch that was sent by Jerko Doko who was the Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a different thing. That was towards the end of April.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts, I would say. And in Prijedor, that dispatch inspired the Serbs to take over power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's move on from the 12th of April to the end of April and let's talk about the second dispatch. That dispatch was sent to us by Delimustafic, the Minister of the Interior and Jerko Doko, the Minister of Defence. It arrived in Prijedor and then every other municipality, and according to that dispatch, the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs were to be attacked with all might.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, all that was denied subsequently. It was a false dispatch that somebody circulated under false pretext.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, there was nothing false about that, and the Trial Chamber will learn that, but is it true that on the 29th or between the 29th and the 30th of April, the Serb side took over power in Prijedor because an attack had been prepared against the JNA and the Serbs in Prijedor? You even just confirmed that for us.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I did not confirm it. There was no attack in the making against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that then, and after that time, an offer was tabled for Prijedor to be split into two municipalities and that the Serbian should consist of the Serbian part called Varos and the Serbian villages, and the Muslims should be the older part of town, Puharska and whatever they are called, Puharska and Muslim villages, hilltops and so on and so forth, do you know that that motion remained on the table until 30th May?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It was a false offer. The map was published by Kozarski Vjesnik and that map caused dissatisfaction among the Serbs as well because that map that was published featured over 70 per cent of Prijedor municipality that had to be given to the Serbs and that contained the most important infrastructure, economic entities, the national park. So all that should have been given to the Serbs, and what was left to the Muslims was a small part in the part of the town of Prijedor where they constituted a majority, and almost none of the large economic entities. Even the Serbs who resided in the central part of the city, in its nucleus, which according to that map should have been allegedly been given to the Muslim municipality, they protested, they called in a radio show, there was an open telephone line for them to call in. And they directly protested against the person who drafted such a map, who composed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There will always be somebody protesting that their village did not become part of the municipality, but don't you write in your book that you were fully aware that companies and businesses would be divided, regardless of whether they are -- where they are located, they would be divided, and you write -- did you imply that the public utilities would remain joint, such as electricity supply and water supply, et cetera? Would it be the only city in Yugoslavia to have more than one municipality?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, you are either paraphrasing or pulling it out of context because I never wrote anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, pause. Please pause. And start again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you do write that they would be divided but let us look at 1D4275 in e-court, to see what Prijedor municipality looks like. And then I would like to ask the AV director to zoom in on the upper left part. We can see where Prijedor is. Can we zoom in on the north west and place it in the centre? You write about that on page 57 of your book. You are fully aware that demands are made to divide companies, schools and organisations that were created from withdrawals from the salaries of all the working people like those working people did not involve -- include Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, Muslims and Croats were not in favour of that division.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers need to pause between question and answer. They are overlapping all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that Muslims and Croats in Prijedor were not in favour of any divisions but they wanted to divide Yugoslavia and they wanted to take Serbs outside of Yugoslavia and make them a national minority.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You said that, not I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you also need to put a pause between the answer and your question. You should be familiar with that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to your Excellency and the interpreters as well, but I'm really trying to get through as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this. You must know by heart every single village here, blue and green.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Sivac, that in Sarajevo, there are ten municipalities, five of which have both one part inside the city and villages outside the city as is the case in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Probably, that may be the case in Sarajevo. All I know about is Prijedor. I can only answer questions about Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many people are there in a municipality? In Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union, the average population is 40.000, in Greece it's 8.000, and Prijedor has more than 100.000, and you still think it shouldn't be divided into several municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: All your games about divisions in Prijedor were aimed at gaining time. If at the level of the republic, at the global level, you realise, and you make a decision to annex the whole of Prijedor to the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina which had already stated they were willing to live only in the former Yugoslavia, or the rump Yugoslavia, then all these games you played at that time, in April, were only moves to win time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are reading your own stuff into our intentions. Do you know that in February of that year, on 14th of February, we had definitively accepted that we would not remain a part of Yugoslavia and we accepted the European community's condition to remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina? It was on the 13th of February. It was all published in the media.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Maybe you paid lip service to all these agreements, but you did everything differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You write that on the 22nd February, we returned from Lisbon, that's page 54, the first discussion on BH held in Lisbon, no result whatsoever. The SDA wanted a totally independent BH; whereas, the SDS suggested a confederation with complete equality between ethnicities. Do you know that Croats were a Catholic community in Bosnia, and they supported the proposal of a confederation with three different entities that was also supported by the European community?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know much about these agreements at the level of the republic. You were involved in higher politics, you negotiated with the international community and with the other politicians in Sarajevo. I can only speak about the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you're also talking about central things and Lisbon and you state, inaccurately, that on that February nothing was achieved. The first step was on 13th of February, the second on the 22nd, the second step, and finally in March, an agreement was made to divide Bosnia into three constituent parts, like it is today, in fact, but it's only two entities instead of three. Did you know about these things?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I just conveyed that information as I found it in a Sarajevo newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you then say that the demand for the transformation of Prijedor was some kind of manoeuvre on our part? If Muslims would have complete authority in all their areas and Serbs would have complete authority in their areas, while sharing some joint bodies, as we do now in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you claim that it was a Serbian game when you would have the same thing as Serbs? You would have government in your own neighbourhoods and areas and you would be in charge of your own affairs.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You were only paying lip service to that sort of suggestion and agreement. All the events that followed showed your real intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Cehajic and other Muslim representatives had accepted that and moved to the left bank of the Sana river and started establishing their own municipality and their own police station?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That too is not true. If that had happened, I would have at least known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You claim that it didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I claim it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did the weapons remain in the hands of Muslims in all these green areas? Did they have check-points at the access roads to each Muslim settlement, all the way until 23rd May?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, when you ask a question, please specify the time and dates relevant to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From 30th of April onwards, when the Serbs took over power in Prijedor to prevent, as you said yourself, whether you believe it or not, to prevent attacks on the army and the Serbs, from the 30th of April until the 23rd of May, is it the case that all the Muslims in their own areas have check-points and have their own weapons without anybody asking them to surrender those weapons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Karadzic. Immediately after the takeover, a call was publicly made for mobilisation. Both the police and the army were reinforced to full complement, and the next move of the new government in Prijedor was to put all the media under their control. On the 12th of May they arrested me and a large number of ham radio operators, private persons who had their own radio stations, properly licensed. The new authorities began to hermetically close the Prijedor municipality and isolate it. Call-ups for mobilisation were sent out to all the Serbs, and at the same time, an announcement was made to all non-Serbs that they must hand in their weapons, failing which they would suffer consequences. All this lasted until the 23rd May, when that incident in Hambarinsko Polje happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that General Talic came, and on the 20th May, there were talks with the local people from Kozarac, that they should take over law enforcement in their own settlement but stay out of fighting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I know that after the takeover in Prijedor municipality, Kozarac, that was 90 per cent populated by Muslims, became a big problem for the new Serb authorities in Prijedor. All sorts of emissaries went to Kozarac to try to convince the local residents to accept the newly installed authorities who had been installed by force, but they did not accept that. They expressed their wish to remain to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aren't you contradicting yourself? You were saying they were trying to convince them by force. You go to force people with tanks, whereas they went to talk.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me. They went to talk, but the Kozarac people did not want to accept the forcible takeover that had happened in Prijedor because they thought, very reasonably, that nothing installed by force could have anything to do with democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs were in power in Prijedor, but they were not the ones who had been planning attacks on the JNA and the Muslims. It was the Muslims who had planned attacks on the JNA and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: The Muslims in Prijedor had no means, no resources, to wage war. If they had the wherewithal, they got the moral right to do it on the 30th of April when the Serbs took over by force, when they disarmed Muslim and Croat policemen. They had the right to react, to try to stop it. However, the Muslims had realised, long since, that they did not have a prayer of defending Prijedor if the Serbs ever decided to take it over by force. Large contingents, large arsenals of weapons, were based in Prijedor and around it, weapons that had been brought from Croatia, and all the other equipment of the former JNA, and I'm underlining that it's former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then whose bright idea was it to move against Serbs who were so well armed? Who opted for war? Isn't it true that you went to Kozarac and Medunjanin did too, and didn't you all advocate that Kozarac should resist?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know where you got that, that I went there. I just heard that as a news item. I didn't go to Kozarac at the time. My reporting and the reporting of my colleague, Boro Grubic, had stopped long before because the IT centre in Banja Luka had been seized by the Serbian Democratic Party, and our communications with our head office were broken. The people in Prijedor were never in favour of any military or war option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But is it true that you wrote in your book, page 109, that Alija Izetbegovic had sent a message not to give up weapons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic kept sending all sorts of messages. Perhaps he sent that one, too. If I wrote that, then he must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in that same book, you qualified the SDA as war mongers, and you say on page 91: "They were pushing people and instigating them into war, but now they are nowhere to be found. They left their people in the lurch on the eve of a great historical battle. They completely lost face." So you were aware that they were going for the war option in defiance of all Serb proposals to keep peace in Prijedor, and it was the leadership of the SDA who were doing that, Mirza Mujadzic, Hilmo Popovac [phoen], and you named the other people who had first instigated people to war and then ran away.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: If you are quoting from my book, then I must have written it, but in a different context. It was a radical branch of the SDA that was a bit trigger-happy. With the help of their Serb friends after the takeover, they escaped somewhere outside of Prijedor and their political activity ceased. The town of Prijedor and the Prijedor municipality were left to their own devices. On one hand, there was you, very well trained and very well armed, with your units and their combat experience from Croatia, and on the other hand there were Muslims and Croats who had almost no weapons at all, apart from a few pieces that they had bought from Serbs who had smuggled some weapons coming back from the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Sivac, that we had no communication with the head office in Prijedor? And you can find that both in my diary and in the speech made by Srdjo Srdic in the assembly, they didn't ask us anything because they couldn't ask us anything. The communications were down?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I was talking about TV links and radio links, but the telephone worked all the time. As for Srdjo Srdic, sometime after 12 May, a colleague of mine came to visit, and he kept me very well informed, and he said that at the famous assembly session in Banja Luka, on the 12th of May, you had a brief encounter with politicians from Prijedor led by Srdjo Srdic and you praised them for having taken over the power in Prijedor without a single shot fired. But you said, However, we have to think of the future. I'm not quoting, of course I'm paraphrasing the best I can. Srdjo Srdic asked, How do you mean that, president? And you said, If in the future we want to join Prijedor municipality as an integral part of this new Serbian state, the international community would probably demand that the population, since it is mixed, declare their wishes, whether they want it or not. And since non-Serbs are the majority, they would probably not want to live in that new Serbian state. And then Srdjan Srdic asked you what to do, and you said, You have all you need. Just make sure to reduce the non-Serb population to a reasonable number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, Mr. Sivac, did you make that up or did somebody else make it up? Do you have an ounce of evidence for what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I got it from a very good friend of mine, who was there, who was present at that meeting, and I believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now, please tell us his name because the defence has the right to check. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I won't say it. I am sure I have the right to withhold it. Unfortunately, he's no longer alive but his family is still there in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean he's a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How very convenient. He's not alive but you are making unbelievable claims. How did you make up that I'm related to Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's what he was boasting about in Prijedor. He didn't actually say he was directly related to you. He said his second wife is somehow related to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. You hear something and then you write it in your book as if it were scripture. Do you stand behind what you wrote in your book and in what you said in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's how it was. You ethnically cleansed Prijedor. You made it so that non-Serbs disappeared from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide. When we collect all the evidence, the Chamber will make their own conclusions about what happened in Prijedor. How did you make up that I am related to the second wife of Srdjo Srdic and that I slept with my entourage of 12 policemen in his apartment rather than the hotel?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I never said you spent the night there with your 12 policemen. Srdjo Srdic bragged, and I was on very good terms with him and with the other man, the journalist, he bragged that you always preferred to spend the night at his place and his wife's place, because you were somehow related. And he was your main political partner in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Sivac, that all the leaders, especially the leaders of major political parties, had official escorts from our joint MUP, official security details, and they never let me spend nights anywhere else but the place chosen by the security detail?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I know, because I worked in the security service at one point, how they treated politicians and how it was all organised. Now, I don't know anything more about this than what I heard from your party member in Prijedor, Srdjo Srdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who set fire to the hotel in Prijedor, Mr. Sivac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Which hotel, Mr. Karadzic? There were two. Do you mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Please, I'm asking you once again, specify the time and date relevant to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, tell me, is it true, and is it beyond any doubt, and you confirmed it in your book, that Muslims attacked Prijedor on the 30th of May from several directions?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that information was taken over from Kozarski Vjesnik, that published a story in several instalments reconstructing what they call the attack on Prijedor, and I call it an attempt to liberate Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's take that it's true. Did this attempt to liberate Prijedor take place on the night of the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: An informal group, including Slavko Ecimovic and some men that, after the takeover, had to escape from Prijedor because the Serbs wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the background. I'm just asking you, is it true that there was an attempt to liberate Prijedor with the use of weapons from several directions on the 30th of May at dawn? Did you listen to the shooting, and did you observe it from your window?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But I took that reconstruction of the attack from the very-well-informed Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper, which, in its turn, falsified some of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say an informal group. These bullets and the rockets fired from "zolja" hand-held launchers, were they also informal or were they controlled by someone?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They were not under anyone's control. They did not belong to the HDZ or the SDA. It was a group of desperate people who were just trying to return to their homes in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside. Let's go back for a moment. Is it true that at the check-point in Hambarine, on the 22nd of May, a car was stopped with four Serbian and two Croatian reservists, six young men in all, two were killed, two were seriously wounded, and two lightly wounded, and the police held Aziz Aliskovic suspect in that incident?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But you failed to say that at the same check-point one man was killed and two were seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was one wounded Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, that's not true. One was killed and two were seriously wounded. And this Ferid Sikiric, who was treated at the hospital after having given an interview, was liquidated by the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any proof of that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. There is evidence, and I presented a lot of material and a lots of videotapes to this Tribunal. There is one videotape where this Ferid Sikiric makes his last statement, and after that he was found in one of the mass graves outside Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So now he's found in a mass grave, and a moment ago you say he was liquidated by the police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they took him away. They killed him and threw his body into one of the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I know because I researched it. I was interested in that case, and I knew the man very well, this Ferid Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you make available that research to us, your own private investigation? How and when did you investigate this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It's not I who investigated it. The Serbian television in Prijedor reported on it, and their report was prepared by Rade Mucic and another Muslim colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just said you researched it.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After the event, I became interested in the fate of this Ferid Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After you were released from the camp, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked a great deal trying to collect documentation about events that happened in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the book, on page 113, you say that telephones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you are moving to another topic, I think it's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can take the break, but I'm still in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in relation to what we discussed briefly in private session, as per your request, we will not be sitting tomorrow, but on Friday, who will we start with? Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. And excluding this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand, Mr. President, although hoping we can complete the witness today. I would imagine that -- well, I thought about that in a couple of permutations but perhaps it's useful if I speak with the Registrar about the videolink issue before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm suggesting -- I'm raising this, that it would be better, it would be in the interest of justice to conclude the witness who will testify via videolink on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suspected that the Registrar would feel the same way, and if the Court feels that way, I am not aware of any circumstances that would trump that concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I think Defence is also following. We will take a break and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, before we recommence can I raise one matter quickly? The Court is aware that I don't normally interfere with the cross-examinations, but this is -- a matter was raised that I simply thought needed to be addressed. The Court is aware, of course, that a -- the counsel needs a good-faith basis for making allegations in the course of the proceedings. Mr. Karadzic suggested, at pages 39 and 40, that the son of Becir Medunjanin had been arrested in the United States as a terrorist, saying, "Did you know that?" In this case, Mr. President, the simplest scrutiny of the internet, from where this information obviously came, would have revealed that the person arrested in the United States for the event Mr. Karadzic referred to had a different name, was 20 years younger, nearly 20 years younger than the son of Becir Medunjanin, had gone to high school in the United States, many, many completely different factors that would have resulted in the elimination of this kind of cross-examination, and the elimination of a canard against the son of Mr. Medunjanin that is unnecessary, and it would be sitting out here if I didn't address it. So I apologise for doing so, but it was just -- given the nature of that allegation against somebody who was already a victim, as we heard, I couldn't let it sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to respond to this or you just -- I would like you to take into -- take what Mr. Tieger said into account in the future cross-examination. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say this: If the sons Adis and Anis [as interpreted], then Anis was indeed arrested under that name, Anis Medunjanin. He was from Bosnia. He was arrested in America as a terrorist. One name is certainly Adis. I'll ask the witness whether Anis was the other name and that's why I thought that that was important, but we'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Nagib, Suljo [phoen], Tadic, Beco, Kanjula [phoen], Medic, did you discuss with them the issue of Kozarac at all?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: What persons are you talking about? I don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Beco is Beco, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin, I never discussed the issue of Kozarac with him. I never talked to him, let alone discussed the issue of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see 1D04348 in e-court? Did you know Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I met Sead Cirkin after the conflict in 1994 -- 5, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there another Sivac who was a prominent activist?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Perhaps you mean Sefik Sivac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see here that on the 2nd of May, a meeting was held to consider the situation in Kozarac. That meeting did not necessarily take place in Kozarac itself, but there is a reference to Sivac and to some other men. Did you ever attend a meeting of that kind?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I've never seen this document before. I never attended any meetings, and especially not on the 2nd May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, we will not follow that line of questioning. Thank you. We will verify this in other ways. Further on in your book you say, and you mention the directions from which the attack came against Prijedor, right? And you also mentioned different groups.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the groups as they were identified by Rade Mutic and Zivko Jakic, both journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that confirmed by Mirzet, whose diary you quote from or you paraphrase, but you mostly quote from in your book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Only partially did he confirm what was written in Kozarski Vjesnik. However, he told me that there were a total of some 60 men, those desperate men from Prijedor, in those groups. They had a few rifles, but most of them carried only pistols, and they tried to enter Prijedor in order to see what could be done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they did enter Prijedor, they came as far as the red high-rise buildings, they almost took the radio building.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it was just a trick to allow them to enter as deep as possible into Prijedor. The military was already at a stand-by, the elite unit under the command of Zoran Karlica. However, Mr. Karadzic, that was a false attack, as you call it, and I call it a liberation -- the liberation of Prijedor, but there are a lot of controversies about that attack or that liberation attempt. When I collected material with this regard, I came by a number of documents, a large number of documents, that proved that that attack had been agreed, had been staged, in order to gain a pretext for the ethnic cleansing of the very nucleus of the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that this was agreed by the Serbs and the Green Berets and their leader, Slavko Ecimovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Again you're pulling things out of their context. Those were no Green Berets at all. They called themselves lads from Kurevo. They did not belong to any political party. They did not belong to any political option, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not write in your book that when the Serbs arrived in Kozarac to negotiate, that they were encircled, surrounded by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that was on the very eve of the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac, and you said it yourself that on the 22nd May, Bosnia-Herzegovina was admitted as a member of the United Nations, and the official symbol of the internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina were lilies, and those people in Kozarac had every right to wear the insignia, the symbols of the state that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: On the Green Berets, they -- and on the Blue Berets, they sported the symbol of lily which was the official symbol of the officially recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to that internationally recognised symbol, you mention the Green Berets in your book but not the Blue Berets. So was that officially recognised symbol accepted by Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm just telling you what the people of Kozarac accepted as their symbol and in Kozarac there were no Serbs or Croats. 97 per cent of the population were Muslims. There was just an insignificant number of Serbs, and you know that in Trnopolje there were some national minorities, the Czechs, Italians, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in your book, you convey parts of Mirzet's diary which confirm that those terrorists or fighters, if we can put it that way, those who wanted to liberate Prijedor, that they got mixed up with the civilian population in Prijedor? You say that in your book on page 128, that they got mixed up with the people, some took to the woods, and some got mixed up with the people in town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. I would like to see that page. I never wrote that. The general resistance put up by the group that attempted to liberate Prijedor was crushed within no more than two hours. Most of the group were arrested. Eighteen people from that group were killed. And only a small number managed to swim across the Sana river and they fled somewhere in the vicinity of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to all the participants in these proceedings how was all that staged? Why did you not write that in the book? You were praising Slavko Ecimovic and the liberators of Prijedor. Why do you not write about the attack being staged and actually arranged between the Serbs and the Muslims? We have to make breaks between questions and answers, so I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I wanted to praise those lads when I was writing the book because they had attempted to save the honour, save the face of Muslims and Croats in Prijedor. Their only wish was to show to the Serbs that Prijedor belonged to the others as well. Slavko Ecimovic, engineer Slavko Ecimovic, was captured alive and killed, but his entire family was also killed in retaliation, his father, his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. You didn't see that. You can't talk about that. But tell me this: You say that you praised them in the book knowing that they participated in a staged attack against Prijedor, that they did a favour to the Serbs by having attacked Prijedor, or are you saying that what you wrote in your book is not true? What is it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. Again you're pulling things out of the context. I did not describe that attack myself. That attack was described by Rade Mutic, Zelko Kesmucic [phoen] in Kozarski Vjesnik. I only conveyed that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look how you conveyed it. On page 129, you describe -- so you say you carry Mirzet's words from his diary. And he says, "There was a plan for us to organise ourselves, and when the conditions were put in place, we would threaten the Serbs that had occupied the city." And then you say, "The first group for the area of Ljubija headed by Bakir Mualjagic [phoen]; the second group will attack Zegari. Slavkovic Muco [phoen] headed the third group." And that's on page 129 of the book, "The third group will attack the territory of Hasrahanovic [phoen], Hambarine, Biscani --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Interpreter's note: We do not have the text in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- just simply impossible to follow on the part of the Judges as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Well, I am in panic because of the time. This witness has testified to a great extent and he has provided a lot of generalised statements. The Defence has to reduce his testimony to the mere and bare facts. That's why I need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 129 of your book, you describe at least four groups that attacked Prijedor from at least four different directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that book in our e-court, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been notified to the parties, to the Prosecution? In my list of documents to be used with this witness, it is not noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a book, almost 300 pages long. It hasn't been translated. I take the opportunity of the witness's presence here for him to be able to either confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One further question for Mr. Robinson is that the line of questioning in relation to this book is to test the credibility of the witness, or -- I'm asking this because it is not the book that was admitted as evidence in this case. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to defer this to Dr. Karadzic because he has a better idea at what he's aiming at than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have been spending more than two hours just on this book which is not evidence in this case. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the witness's testimony is evidence. He testified in the Stakic case, and what he said there differs from what he has written in the book, when he could do it at his own pace. The book is relevant because it proves that there was an attack, that he knew about it, and it is contrary to what he testified so far, and I'm also testing his credibility. You've seen the attitude of Muslims and Croats who wanted to go on living with the Serbs. You saw the attitude towards me, he calls me a werewolf. This is all relevant because he is the author of the book. We have the author in front of us and he confirms everything knowing that I have the book in front of me. Maybe I can provide him with a copy. I can print -- give him a print-out of the book, but he should know it by heart. He should know what he wrote in his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Prosecution has been provided with a copy of the book at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The book was originally within our files, so yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I see what you say, but you could achieve the same object by choosing - I pluck a figure from the air - half a dozen of the best points as illustrative. You really don't have to go through the whole book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. I believe this shows my inexperience. I'm much worried about the things that I'd fail to touch upon and shed some light. In my view, I did enough to show, expose the nature of this evidence, although I'm not convinced the Chamber shares my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having described these four groups at page 129?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this was carried from the Kozarski Vjesnik. The two men involved were well acquainted with the investigations following the failed attempt. They described the events, including the groups. It was for the first time that I learned of the existence of those four groups at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you quote Mirzet and not Rade Mutic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was freed in 1993, I met Mirzet in Zagreb. I knew him well. We discussed those events in Prijedor between the 30th of May and the 1st of June. He shed some light on these events, and he informed me that one of them was instructed by someone in the Prijedor barracks, and he took others along, claiming that they should liberate Prijedor and that they would be awaited by 500 armed citizens who would welcome them. Only a few days later before, the Serb TV had some footage on their news of Muslim citizens from Puharska and Biscani, handed over their weapons voluntarily in the Prijedor barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So indeed, at page 129, you quote Mirzet, and you even say Mirzet went on to say, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know my book by heart, but you are paraphrasing many of the things. You are not quoting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 132, do you also mention some information received from him, that they used a hand-held rocket launcher to set fire to the Prijedor hotel?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The group that entered Prijedor had only two operational hand-held rocket launchers. They had another two which malfunctioned and they had bought them from Serb middle men. They used one to target a hotel in Prijedor which housed an elite unit from the Knin Krajina which assisted the process of the takeover of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say that those people were jumping out the windows when the hotel caught fire?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, that's what Mirzet said. But no one was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D04347 in e-court? Your Excellencies, perhaps I can explain why I'm following the book. It goes in parallel with this man's testimony. It addresses the same topics but in a different way. That is why I'm interested in the book. Mr. Sivac, do you see that this comes from the Prijedor security service on the 22nd June, 1992? It is a criminal report submitted to the Prosecutor, the document specifies those involved. Could we please go to the next page in English? We can even leaf through the document and there is a total of 28 -- no, in total, there are 172; whereas, you said there were 20 to 30. So 172 persons who were identified and reported.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: What was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by what you said, which is that Prijedor was attacked by a group of 20 to 30 rather than the men contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I said already that together with Slavko Ecimovic there were some 20. With Kemo Divjak, there were another 20. They were organised in groups, and their goal was to assemble and try to reach the territory of Bosnian Krajina, which was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They meant to go as far as Bihac and Bosanska Krupa. The truth is that there were around 80 of them. This figure of yours is incorrect. It is a fabrication. If you wish, I can discuss the names of the people I recognise on the list. This indictment was issued on the 22nd June, 1992. By that time, Nedzad Babic had been killed. Asmir Muhic had been killed by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can't take your word for it, witness. If you have no proof. Could we please have page 7 in Serbian and 13 in English? You say that no Serbs were killed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: During that operation in Prijedor there were some killed Serbs. I didn't say anything otherwise. I accept your argument that some Serbs were killed in the conflict. What I did say was that during the incident at the hotel, no one was killed, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the statement of reasons. Following the carrying out of all necessary preparations and assessments of the situation, on 30th of May 1992, the -- those mentioned in the document carried out an armed attack by having reached Prijedor together and then broke into four groups: The first group was to target the Municipal Assembly building and the public security stations; the second was to go to the hotel and Radio Prijedor; the third was to capture the area around the flyover and they were supposed to link up with another group at that location. I don't think this is the right page in English. We have it now. So four groups are being mentioned. To conclude the paragraph, it says: "By which they would prevent the army leaving the garrison to defend the town." It is also stated that they killed 18 and wounded 15 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. Far fewer were killed. The Serb media said that there were 18 people killed and that there may have been around 15 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. The media is one thing. But this is a document, a criminal report to the Prosecutor, do you think the police would dare send incorrect information to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know if they dared or not. In any case, I disagree with it. This list includes people who were not part of the group at all or the groups. I know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain, then, how the Serbs staged the whole thing to include the 11 killed Serbs? How did they manage to organise four Muslim groups and get them to attack Prijedor and have Serbs killed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I believe the Serbs who were killed were collateral damage. I seem to have read a document here in which Simo Drljaca asked that the snipers, the sharp shooters, be withdrawn from key positions in order not to prevent the entry of those groups to Prijedor. I'm convinced that the attack or the attempted liberation was staged. Many of the people on this list did not take part in the attack on Prijedor. These people were simply added on to the list in order to show that there were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please go to the previous page to see the person number 172? The page before. There we can see that the list includes 172 participants.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'd love to see the whole list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I only see people from 156 to 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have a look at that. We can only have one page at a time.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let's go to the beginning of the list, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe I can help. I think we can probably print that document up and then it could be handed to the witness, given that he's asked to have a look at the list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's only 13 pages, the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is even less in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You may be right in one thing, and that is that the numbers in the Serbian are different because people were included there. As you say in your book, did your nephew choose to keep his arms and join the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, it was a relative of mine. His name was Adnan. He was part of the police reserve force. And he was close friends with Slavko Ecimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were each other's witnesses at weddings, at their weddings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, and classmates too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slavko Ecimovic, to remind the Chamber, is the one who led the operation in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the Muslim villages surrounding Prijedor, there were units in each of the villages and that they had dugouts, radios. In any case, is it true that they had dugouts and that they stayed there for a while?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That is not correct. This is again some kind of virtual information you only seem to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you touch upon that in your book when you said that they had powerful radio equipment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: These were Serb rumours in order to accuse Muslims of something that they were not guilty of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far was the front line from Prijedor, any front line, say towards the corridor or to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: There was no front line in Prijedor. There were no clashes. There was no war. As for any other front lines, well, it all depends on the time period. Do you mean in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 30th of May. This is what you wrote about. Was the front line hundreds of kilometres away at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did the Serbs have fortifications around their houses in Prijedor as well as sandbags? This is something you mentioned as well in your book.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Because the Serbs in Prijedor were constantly being explained by Radio Prijedor that next to Prijedor, or in its vicinity, there were several thousand Mujahedin and a number of foreign mercenaries. They were also told that there were some sort of elite units surrounding Prijedor ready to carry out massacres in and around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in depth, Mr. Sivac, hundreds of kilometres in the back of the Prijedor Brigade, weren't there such groups indeed killing farmers at work, who had dugouts, and who communicated among each other?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: There were no paramilitary Muslim or Croatian units in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll discuss it further later down the road. Was the HOS or the HVO present in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What if I told you that we have Croatian intercepts, they tapped in on our conversations, and they explain in detail the battle in Kozarac and Prijedor, they discuss 3.000 captured Muslim soldiers? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, that's what you say. I have never heard of any HOS or HVO members in Prijedor. Another fabrication, it seems, in order to justify what had been done in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we -- I'd like to tender this document, please, and, witness, please look at the names in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I know that some of these people were killed during the attempted liberation of Prijedor. Some were taken to camps and that would be it. On the 30th of May, the group was neutralised in less than two hours. Following that, there was a systematic process of destruction in Prijedor. The entry of Slavko's group was an excuse to ethnically cleanse the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You discuss ethnic cleansing, whereas we had Muslims from the nearby villages streaming into Prijedor. How do you reconcile these two things?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You're twisting things again. When the ethnic cleansing began in Kozarac, only a small number of Kozarac people arrived in Prijedor. And they were accommodated with their friends in Puharska. After a short while, an ultimatum was issued by the authorities that even those people had to be evacuated to Trnopolje immediately. In the area of Prijedor, when the ethnic cleansing began --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do not go into that. How do you explain what you're saying? What is ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing is this: When one group uses pressure, force, police, in order to destroy two other ethnic groups, people of other religious beliefs, of other cultures, who prayed to different gods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you say in your book that people left Prijedor even before the war and after the crisis, that they sought ways to leave, to be put on the list to be sold a plane ticket, that they were very determined to do so although their families were against it and they tried to convince them not to leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: A number of inhabitants of Prijedor who could no longer bear the situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking for any explanations. I'm asking you this: On page 221 of your book, did you say that Lejla, Alma and Sena from your brother's family wanted to leave? Their friends, relatives, and neighbours wanted to dissuade them but they were determined? Did you not write throughout the entire book that everybody was looking to purchase a plane ticket to Belgrade and from there onwards to Europe?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You're again distorting the facts, and again you're putting me several questions in one. First of all, there were those who wanted to purchase plane tickets to Belgrade to travel further afield into the world. That was before the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do not throw terms at me. I'm asking you about events and not about ethnic cleansing. Do not give me any qualifications. I'm not going to allow you the same thing that was allowed to you in the Stakic case. You have to be very precise. Please leave ethnic cleansing aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to be precise first in putting your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking for the witness to refrain from qualifications. It is up to the Trial Chamber to put qualifications to different events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to put such a question, you have to put the book to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you write this? They tried to dissuade them but they were determined and there were many such people who were determined to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there are two questions in one. What you asked me about now happened in September 1992. That's why I would like you to give me the date and the place where those things happened. In September 1992, when the convoys of Bosniaks started leaving Prijedor, Alma and Sena who were members of my cousin Omer's family, they knew that Omer and Adnan had been killed in Omarska. There were two other members of their family. And that's when they decided to join a convoy and to head for central Bosnia and the territory under the control of the BiH Army. And let me now go back to your first question. Your first question was whether people left Prijedor by plane. No, they didn't, because Prijedor does not have an airport. People from Prijedor would go to Banja Luka first and those departures by plane happened before April. They took place in March and April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the conflicts broke out, did people still want to leave?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: When the conflicts broke out, nobody could move out from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unless there was an agreement to arrange a convoy, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Only later, towards the end of August. The first people started to move out by way of convoys organised by the Red Cross from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, but not in your book, you claim that the private property was taken over and that the ownership titles were changed. Give me an example. Can you illustrate the change of the ownership title of property in an illegal way? Give me an example of a sale of property because that was also forbidden during the war, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, that was you paying lip service to things. However, in Prijedor, strange things happened. A large amount of private assets were misappropriated by the Serbs, because the Court and the services that were in charge of that did a very lackluster job. Fortunately enough, after the Dayton Accords were signed, and after people started returning to Prijedor, many managed to reinstate their assets that had been illegally taken away from them. However, there are still people, even today, in Prijedor, who have not managed to reinstate their personal property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If a refugee is found in a Muslim part of Bosnia, I am sure that they had difficulties. But give me just one example of somebody's property being illegally misappropriated. Just one example?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: One example is the example of my colleague. I don't know if I'm allowed to mention his name. He was one of the richest people in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's up to you whether you're allowed to mention the name or not. What was taken from him, and who did it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: He was a very rich citizen of Prijedor and his property was misappropriated by his former colleague. He was the owner of a company, and he and that other person simply registered the company in his name. After the year 1995, when the original owner returned to Prijedor for the first time, after the war, he had to find witnesses, and he had to resort to certain legal institutions in order to prove that that was his property and not the property of the latter person who wanted to misappropriate his assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that somebody misappropriated his assets?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And while my colleague was in a camp, and while he was being transferred from the camp into one of the third countries, a Serb colleague in the Prijedor court falsified his documents and almost misappropriated his assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's not talk about individuals falsifying documents. I want to know what the state was doing at the time. Was it the state that systematically misappropriated other people's property?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: You asked me for one example and I gave you one example. Please don't be cross with me. The state was also systematically engaged in the misappropriation of assets. For my family, for example, for my family to leave Prijedor, we had to sign 15 different documents, one of them was to the effect that we are relinquishing the right on all of our immovable property, and that's when we were able to get the final certificate to be able to move out from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the other 14 documents?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Those were documents as a means to take money from the other Croats and Bosniaks who wanted to leave Prijedor. You had to provide 14 documents in order to get -- obtain the final certificate allowing you to leave. And those documents were to prove that you paid all your dues, all your bills, all your electricity, water, that your car was deposited with the SUP as war booty. I really can't remember all of those documents. It had to be furnished, they had to be collected, and taken to the military department where you would then obtain your final certificate to the effect that you had paid all your dues and as a result of that you are allowed to move out from the Republika Srpska. My wife had to obtain all those certificates from the military department for our children, for my son who was 6 and my daughter who was 11, at the moment when we decided to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that you had to surmount many obstacles before you were able to move out?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, those obstacles did exist but they were erected deliberately in order to ferret out whatever little money we had left because all those documents you had to pay for. Let me give you a trivial example. For somebody to cancel their electricity account, they had to pay their bills in advance for a year, a year in advance. And even people whose houses had been burned down or destroyed had to do the same thing. Why would anybody want to pay electricity a year in advance for the house that doesn't even exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, there were many obstacles and it was very difficult to obtain all those documents?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Not because of the political situation. Because of the money that you had to pay. They wanted to ferret out every little -- every last cent that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please send the Prosecutor's office all those documents and certificates that you have just described for us?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what I'm saying is this: In order to obtain your final certificate allowing you to move out, you had to furnish all of those documents. I still keep that certificate for my family, for my 6 year old son and 11 year old daughter, issued by the military department. What did the military department have to do with my minor children? But I still keep those certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm talking about the documents, the 14 documents, not about the final certificate, but the 14 documents that you had to collect and can you provide us with those, and can you tell us whether your property was misappropriated or not? I'm talking about movable property?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, all the documents had to be handed over to the military department. Maybe you should ask your associates to look for those documents that are probably filed in the archives of the military department. What we ended up with was just one final certificate allowing us to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How big is the public security station in Prijedor? What is its foot plan?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It has two wings, two floors on one side, three floors on the other side. There is an annex that was later added on. What is the time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The time frame is May 1992.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, how big was the police station?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I didn't measure it. It was a very typical building of the kind that was used by the police stations everywhere in Prijedor, Brcko, and elsewhere as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how big was the Detention Unit? How many people could be detained at any one time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: At any one time the Detention Unit could hold a dozen people, between 10 and 15. It was a small room because the Prijedor security service did not have a prison. It was just a Detention Unit from which after the sentencing, before the misdemeanour court, the detainees were taken to the prison in Banja Luka. There was a prison in Banja Luka, and that's where people who were detained in Prijedor were taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 10th of June, you were erroneously taken into custody because you shared a similar name with somebody else. They were looking for Nusret but they brought you in, and then you were returned home as soon as the mistake was spotted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you were taken into custody again on 20th of June. You spoke about that and you wrote about that. Do you remember that people were brought in gradually? For example, one man is brought in and then somebody else, after a certain time, from the same circle?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were told that you would be in Keraterm -- or rather in Omarska for only a short period of time, that you would be interviewed, and that then that you would then be sent either home or somewhere else or to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you told when you were first brought in that you would not stay long?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. Who could have told us that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll find it and I will tell you who told you that. Or who was in a position to tell you that. And you were brought to Keraterm only once, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Omarska, who was it who interviewed prisoners in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: There were interviewers who were known to me. They were inspectors of the security service in Prijedor, and there were also interviewers who had worked in the state security detachment in Prijedor. There were also people from the business life who were reservists in the security service, and there were also two inspectors who arrived directly from the State Security Service in Banja Luka. They were the ones who interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. I propose to adjourn for the day. Mr. Sivac, I have to ask you whether, in relation to the scheduling matter, when conducting the proceedings of this size and case, there are many things arising during the course of the hearing. Due to the situations, we are not able to sit tomorrow, and on Friday, there is a witness we have to hear via videolink which is fixed for that day, so therefore I'm inquiring of you whether it would cause you a lot of problem whether you have to continue the remaining evidence Monday -- on Monday next week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is somewhat surprising, I must say. I've been here for a long time but I'm in your hands, Your Honours. I'll do whatever you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we appreciate it very much. But Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think we exchanged e-mails with the court officer and the Defence was involved too, and we offered our best observations about the circumstances. Of course, we remain optimistic, perhaps unduly so, that we can complete the testimony of both on Friday, but I certainly understand the possibility of the need to continue on Monday and understand why the Court raised the issue. Other than that, I -- it appears to me that the parties are in agreement about tomorrow and about the videolink priority first thing on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the legal officer could approach the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I tender this, Excellency, the last document that was on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton? SJB Prijedor document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For what it's worth, Mr. President, I imagine it's been conveyed to you, I suggested a couple of potential efficiencies that might eliminate a run-over into Monday. Again that depends on a variety of factors, but to the extent the Court's in a position to implement those, we would encourage that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I asked the Chamber's legal officer to liaise with the witness via Victims and Witness Section to sort it out in the best interests of the witness, but what is certain is that we start off with the videolink testimony on Friday. And do you have any objection to the admission of that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we will give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D4347 shall be given Exhibit D1741, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, before we rise I just wanted to first of all thank the witness for his accommodation of our schedule, and secondly to apologise to the Prosecution and the Chamber for not having notified his book because that definitely should have been done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would join in that. I think all of us share the appreciation for the witness's flexibility and willingness to accommodate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, the Chamber does really appreciate your understanding, kind understanding. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of September, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
